title: Mayrath v. Commissioner
articleTitle: Foundations of Innovation: A Forensic Analysis of Mayrath v. Commissioner and the Evolving Jurisprudence of the U.S. Research and Development Tax Credit
subject: Section 174 Research Expenditures
summary: Mayrath v. Commissioner (41 T.C. 582, 1964; aff'd 357 F.2d 209, 5th Cir. 1966) held that an inventor could not deduct the excess costs of building his experimental Dallas family residence as IRC § 174 research expenses. For U.S. taxpayers claiming the IRC § 41 R&D credit, it confirms qualifying research costs require a trade-or-business nexus, investigative purpose, and substantiation.

body.text: Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural Posture and Overview of the Dispute

The decisions of the United States Tax Court in Mayrath v. Commissioner, 41 T.C. 582 (1964), and the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit in Mayrath v. Commissioner, 357 F.2d 209 (5th Cir. 1966), represent a foundational pillar of federal tax jurisprudence governing research and experimental (R&E) expenditures under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 174 and, by statutory incorporation, the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under IRC § 41. Decided initially by Judge Dawson in the Tax Court on January 28, 1964, and affirmed on February 17, 1966, by a unanimous Fifth Circuit panel (Circuit Judges Gewin and Bell, with Senior Judge Jones of the United States Court of Claims, sitting by designation, writing the opinion), the litigation arose from joint federal individual income tax returns filed on a calendar-year, cash-accounting basis by Martin Mayrath and Rose Mayrath for the taxable years 1955, 1956, and 1957.

In the initial statutory notice of deficiency, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue determined income tax deficiencies against the petitioners of $12,265.71 for 1955, $42,107.33 for 1956, and $26,933.46 for 1957. Prior to and during the Tax Court proceedings, the Commissioner agreed that the petitioners had substantiated $44,926.74 of miscellaneous business expenses across twelve distinct classifications, while the petitioners conceded that the Commissioner had properly disallowed $16,500.56 of claimed deductions. Following the Tax Court's entry of decision under Rule 50, the recomputed deficiencies appealed to and affirmed by the Fifth Circuit stood at $5,687.23 for 1955, $33,029.13 for 1956, and $17,019.67 for 1957.
Factual Background and the Taxpayer's Claims

The substantive controversy centered on whether Martin Mayrath, an established inventor of agricultural machinery, could deduct under IRC § 174 the excess construction costs of building a custom, non-wood luxury family residence in Dallas, Texas, alongside collateral deductions under IRC §§ 162 and 167 for engineering services, partial business use of three personal residences, and depreciation on an adjacent workshop. After graduating from Kansas State College in 1932 and holding various positions in automobile and insurance sales, accounting, and as a recorder and computer for the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey, Mayrath assumed operation of his family's Kansas farm in 1939, where he began experimenting with mechanical grain augers. In 1944, Mayrath and his brothers commenced commercial manufacturing and sales of these augers. He secured a United States patent for a grain auger in 1949—alongside foreign patents in Argentina, Australia, and Canada—and between 1951 and 1963 obtained additional United States patents covering mobile power-operated conveyors, articulated conveyor apparatuses, conveyor trough joints, and auger conveyor carriages.

During the tax years at issue, Mayrath owned, directly or indirectly, all the stock of six corporate entities engaged in manufacturing, distributing, and selling agricultural equipment: Mayrath Machinery Co., Inc., Mayrath, Inc., Mayrath Co., Mayrath Southern Co., Mayrath, Ltd., and Mayrath Corp.. Out of approximately $530,000.00 in total gross receipts reported by the petitioners across 1955, 1956, and 1957, roughly $485,000.00 derived directly from transactions with these six agricultural machinery corporations, consisting of patent sale proceeds, interest on patent and loan balances, and executive compensation. Outside of farm implements, Mayrath pursued sporadic concepts for which no patent applications were pending—including a "beep transmitter" for retrieving lost animals or children, an automatic lawn flooding system, and a "musicolor system" for printing orchestral music, which the Tax Court described as totally unrelated to his primary interest in farm implements—and he also held an interest in Christopher Music Co., a music-publishing venture organized in 1953 that was practically dormant during the years in issue and yielded only $719.00 in gross receipts across the entire three-year audit period.

In 1956, Mayrath commenced construction of a two-story, 5,826-square-foot personal residence at 10707 Lennox Lane in Dallas, Texas, completing the structure in 1957 at a total cost of $287,474.11. The residence featured six bedrooms, five bathrooms, a large entrance hall, a living room, a dining room, a bar, a kitchen, an accessory room, a carport, an equipment room, a swimming pool with a bath house and cabana-type sitting area, and a tennis court. Contending that he was engaged in the broad trade or business of "inventing," Mayrath designed the structure as a "house containing no wood," built on concrete piers and steel columns with poured-in-place concrete slabs and using glass, plastics, aluminum, and steel in lieu of wood; the Tax Court assumed that in doing so he mastered some of the construction problems involved, but found that many of the so-called "experimental" features were catalog or luxury items. He paid $4,000.00 in specialized contractor accounting fees during construction to track what he characterized as "special construction" costs.

To compute his tax return deductions under IRC § 174 for 1956 and 1957, Mayrath estimated that a conventional luxury house of comparable size without experimental features could be built for $116,520.00. Treating the $170,954.11 by which the total outlay of $287,474.11 exceeded this $20-per-square-foot baseline as the portion attributable to experimentation, he deducted the same ratio of each year's construction expenditures (59.3 percent, or $73,925.37, for 1956, computed on an estimated total cost of $286,000.00, plus $4,000.00 of contractor accounting expense; and 59.5 percent, or $96,872.40, for 1957), for a total house-related deduction of $174,797.77 across 1956 and 1957—separate from the standalone R&E claims of $2,022.62 in 1956 and $1,904.43 in 1957—as current research and experimental deductions. In addition, Mayrath claimed unresolved business expense deductions across 1955 through 1957 for business services ($400.00 in 1955), engineering and technical services ($3,350.00 in 1955), and pro-rata business use of three personal residences located in California and on Cinderella Lane and Lennox Lane in Dallas ($1,072.96 in 1955, $3,072.46 in 1956, and $3,365.40 in 1957), which included $700.00 and $2,100.00 in depreciation for 1956 and 1957, respectively, on an adjacent office and shop building that he testified, without supporting documentary evidence, had cost $42,000.00.

body.text: The Commissioner's Challenge and Governing Statutory Framework

The Commissioner disallowed the residence deduction on the stated ground that it did not constitute a research and experimental expense within the meaning of the Code, and the litigation turned on four interlocking statutory issues under the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. First, under IRC § 174(a)(1), a taxpayer may treat R&E expenditures as deductible expenses (for domestic research in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, now under IRC § 174A as enacted by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of July 4, 2025, which restored immediate expensing after the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act's capitalization-and-amortization regime, while foreign research expenditures remain subject to 15-year amortization under IRC § 174) only if they are paid or incurred "in connection with his trade or business". The Government asserted that the construction of the house was a personal expense with no connection to Mayrath's trade or business, and the Tax Court found that—whatever the status of his farm-implement inventing—building an "experimental" house for his own family's occupancy could not be considered part of any trade or business, because he was not in the trade or business of constructing residences.

Second, IRC § 174(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(2) and (4)—which the Tax Court set out, and on which the Commissioner relied before the Fifth Circuit, which found it unnecessary to reach the issue—bar § 174 treatment for expenditures for the acquisition or improvement of land, or of property to be used in connection with the research or experimentation that is of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation under IRC § 167. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), qualifying expenditures are strictly confined to "research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense". Where research results in depreciable property, the regulations restrict eligibility to the conceptual and investigative research phase, excluding the costs of component materials, labor, and actual construction.

Third, the Tax Court concluded that the residence construction costs were non-deductible "personal, living, or family expenses" under IRC § 262—which bars such deductions except as otherwise expressly provided—and that Mayrath had failed to show that his unsubstantiated residence-use expenses were other than personal. Fourth, regarding the collateral claims under IRC § 162 (ordinary and necessary business expenses) and IRC § 167 (workshop depreciation), the Tax Court held that Mayrath failed his evidentiary burden of proof to substantiate the expenditures or connect them to a particular trade or business or specific project, and the Fifth Circuit later held that this failure precluded judicial estimation under Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930).

In contemporary United States tax practice, Mayrath v. Commissioner transcends its mid-century origins because IRC § 41—whose credit was originally enacted in 1981 to incentivize incremental research investments, and whose current four-part definition of qualified research in § 41(d) was added by the Tax Reform Act of 1986—establishes in § 41(d)(1)(A) (which, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, refers to expenditures treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A) the "Section 174 Test" as the mandatory threshold prong of the four-part definition of "qualified research". To claim the R&D tax credit under IRC § 41, a taxpayer must demonstrate that the expenditures qualify under IRC § 174 (the Section 174 test), that the research is undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature (the technological information test), that the application of that information is intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component of the taxpayer (the business component test), and that substantially all of the research activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose relating to function, performance, reliability, or quality (the process of experimentation test). Because the Tax Court in Mayrath (41 T.C. at 590) articulated the authoritative judicial interpretation of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2—holding that the statute is intended "to limit deductions to those expenditures of an investigative nature expended in developing the concept of a model or product"—federal courts and the Internal Revenue Service routinely deploy Mayrath to police the boundary between eligible conceptual experimentation and ineligible commercial construction, capital asset fabrication, or routine production.
The Courts' Final Holdings

The United States Tax Court ruled in favor of the Commissioner on every contested issue, and the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed that decision in all matters. In the Tax Court, Judge Dawson held that the excess construction costs of the Lennox Lane residence were neither incurred in connection with a trade or business nor of a research or experimental nature within the intendment of IRC § 174, characterizing them instead as personal living expenses barred by IRC § 262. The Tax Court observed that allowing a taxpayer who professes to be an inventor to deduct the construction costs of a personal family residence under the guise of experimentation would plainly violate the spirit and intent of IRC § 174 and produce an absurd statutory result. All remaining deductions for engineering services, business services, standalone R&E, residential business usage, and workshop depreciation were likewise disallowed for lack of substantiation and failure to prove a nexus to any specific business project.

On appeal, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the Tax Court's judgment in all respects. Applying the "clearly erroneous" standard of appellate review to the Tax Court's factual findings (Higgins v. Commissioner; Loco Realty Co. v. Commissioner), Senior Judge Jones concluded that the Tax Court was not clearly erroneous in finding that Mayrath did not intend to profit from building his own personal house, so that his expenses were not connected with a trade or business; the Fifth Circuit expressly declined to reach the separate questions of whether the expenditures were research or experimental in nature or were barred by IRC § 174(c). Furthermore, the Fifth Circuit decisively rejected Mayrath's invocation of the Cohan rule across both the § 174 house expenditures and the §§ 162 and 167 residential and workshop claims, holding that the fact-finder need not approximate a minimum allowable deduction where the taxpayer fails the threshold burden of proving that any portion of the underlying expenditures was definitely deductible as a bona fide business or research expense.
Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures
Absence of Trade or Business Nexus and Commercial Profit Motive

The primary legal failure that invalidated Mayrath's IRC § 174 claim was the absence of an objective nexus between the construction of the non-wood house and an existing, profit-motivated trade or business. Under IRC § 174(a)(1), R&E expenditures must be incurred "in connection with [the taxpayer's] trade or business". Relying on its prior precedent in John F. Koons, 35 T.C. 1092 (1961), the Tax Court enforced the strict rule that the statutory phrase "trade or business" presupposes an existing business with which the taxpayer is directly connected during the taxable year; expenditures for research and experimentation that are preliminary to the establishment of a business do not qualify; the Fifth Circuit, for its part, rejected Mayrath's contention that he was simply pursuing his "inventive bent," and the Tax Court observed that there is a point beyond which an inventor's propensity to experiment takes on the characteristics of a hobby. While the Supreme Court later relaxed the pre-operating barrier for dedicated start-up ventures with an unmistakable commercial trajectory in Snow v. Commissioner, both the Tax Court and the Fifth Circuit in Mayrath focused on the complete absence of commercial intent and profit motive, which remains fatal under both IRC § 174 and IRC § 41.

As the Fifth Circuit emphasized, invoking Wiles v. United States, a bona fide profit motive is the essence of any trade or business, and the persistent absence of commercial revenues or active commercialization efforts constitutes cogent evidence that no trade or business exists. While Mayrath proved he was an established inventor and corporate executive in the agricultural equipment sector—generating $485,000.00 of his $530,000.00 gross receipts from his six farm machinery corporations—his prior building experience was limited to assisting in the planning and designing of factories, warehouses, and offices for those wholly owned agricultural entities. He had never been engaged in the construction business for profit.

The evidentiary record revealed multiple objective indicators that negated any commercial profit motive in the Lennox Lane project. First, no research was done before construction began to determine whether a market in fact existed for the innovations Mayrath had in mind, no action was taken during construction or immediately thereafter to exploit any of the house's ideas, designs, or features, and only scant records were kept for any commercial application. Second, despite his extensive history of patenting grain augers and conveyors across multiple jurisdictions, almost all of his patents related to farm implements and none of them related to the business of housing construction. Third, immediately upon completion of the residence in 1957, Mayrath moved his family into the 5,826-square-foot home and occupied it continuously as a personal luxury dwelling. Fourth, he made no effort to market, license, or commercialize the non-wood construction concepts until three years after the house was finished—an effort that consisted of a July 1, 1960 letter to seven metal and steel manufacturers (with follow-up correspondence that produced no agreements), sent at about the same time the Internal Revenue Service was auditing his returns for the years at issue, and which the Fifth Circuit described as "token" at best.

To illustrate the evidentiary threshold required to prove a bona fide R&D trade or business, the Fifth Circuit explicitly contrasted Mayrath's self-serving post-audit rationalizations with two landmark taxpayer victories: Kenneth Reiner, 24 T.C.M. 1005, and Best Universal Lock Co., 45 T.C. 1. In Kenneth Reiner, the taxpayer successfully deducted R&E expenditures incurred in constructing an experimental house because the evidentiary record demonstrated an overriding commercial profit motive: there were oral and written agreements between the partners concerning the business venture of constructing an experimental residence, patent counsel was used continually during construction to keep records of potentially patentable developments (20 to 30 preliminary patent applications had been prepared, 10 more had been filed, and 2 patents had issued), one person was employed full time to evaluate the market potential of the ideas, one development was already being produced and sold, detailed records of expenses and materials were maintained, and—crucially—the taxpayer purchased another residence rather than moving into the house, which as of 1963 was still being used strictly for research. Similarly, in Best Universal Lock Co., R&E deductions for a lock manufacturer's work on an isothermal air compressor were sustained because the company's founder experimented on the compressor in the company laboratory and granted the company a nonexclusive license to manufacture and use it, and the evidence strongly showed that he worked on it solely for business purposes and that the company fully intended to exploit his developments. Mayrath's project lacked every single one of these objective commercial indicia.
The Investigative Nature Doctrine Versus Actual Construction and Depreciable Property Exclusions

Even if Mayrath had established a valid trade or business in residential construction, his claim suffered from a second, independent legal defect: the conflation of physical asset construction with investigative research. At 41 T.C. 582, 590 (1964), Judge Dawson examined the scope of IRC § 174(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)-(b), pronouncing the legal standard that has governed R&D tax controversies for over six decades: IRC § 174 is intended "to limit deductions to those expenditures of an investigative nature expended in developing the concept of a model or product". Applying that standard, the court doubted that the petitioners' expenditures for the "actual construction" of their "model" residence were of such an investigative nature, and it faulted their method for failing to assure that the costs of materials, labor, and other component elements of construction were excluded.

This judicial doctrine operates through the interaction of IRC § 174(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(2) and (4). Under IRC § 174(c), Section 174 does not apply to any expenditure for the acquisition or improvement of land, or for the acquisition or improvement of property to be used in connection with research or experimentation that is of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation under IRC § 167 (or IRC § 168 in modern law). While depreciation allowances themselves on dedicated research equipment may be treated as § 174 expenditures to the extent the asset is actually used in qualified research, the capital outlay to construct or acquire the depreciable facility is statutorily excluded. Furthermore, under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(4), even where investigative research is undertaken to develop depreciable property for use in the taxpayer's own trade or business, allowable R&E expenditures are limited to the portion of the expenditures attributable to research, excluding the costs of the component materials, the costs of labor or other elements involved in construction and installation, and costs attributable to the acquisition or improvement of the property.

The second- and third-order implications of Mayrath's "investigative nature" doctrine permeate modern IRC § 41 R&D tax credit litigation across the United States. Because IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) mandates that qualified research expenses (QREs) must first qualify as expenses under IRC § 174, the IRS and the Tax Court apply Mayrath to disqualify projects that fail to prove genuine technological uncertainty and a scientific process of experimentation. Under modern Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1) and IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), activities are only of an "investigative nature" if the taxpayer faces genuine technological uncertainty at the outset regarding capability, method, or appropriate design, and resolves that uncertainty through a methodical process of experimentation fundamentally relying on the hard sciences—engineering, computer science, or the physical or biological sciences. As demonstrated in Max v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-37—which relied directly on Mayrath, 41 T.C. at 590—mastering routine fabrication or design challenges using known engineering or craft techniques lacks the investigative character and scientific hypothesis testing required by the statute. In Mayrath, although the Tax Court assumed that in building a "house containing no wood" the taxpayer had mastered some of the construction problems involved, it found that many of the so-called "experimental" features were catalog or luxury items and that the special problems encountered were often the result of unusual combinations of materials, modifications of standard construction principles, or the use in residential construction of features commonly used in commercial construction.

Furthermore, Mayrath governs the disallowance of commercial production, supply, and depreciable prototype costs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), which explicitly excludes land and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation from "supplies used in the conduct of qualified research". In Chief Counsel Advice (CCA) 200013017 and cases such as Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, and Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, the IRS and federal courts have drawn the same line between investigative research and ordinary production that Mayrath, 41 T.C. at 590–591, articulated—most prominently in Union Carbide, where the Tax Court and the Second Circuit denied supply QREs for raw materials that would have been purchased for production regardless of the research—although those rulings rest principally on the statutory and regulatory supply rules rather than on Mayrath itself, and in Little Sandy Coal the Seventh Circuit held that pilot-model production costs are not categorically excluded from the "substantially all" calculation. While Treasury Decision (T.D.) 9680 (effective July 21, 2014) amended Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) to clarify that the costs of constructing a "pilot model"—defined as any representation or model of a product produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement—can qualify under IRC § 174 even if the pilot model is eventually sold or used in production, the Tax Court has since emphasized (in Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, involving custom-built air pollution control systems) that the taxpayer must show how a claimed pilot model was actually used to evaluate and resolve uncertainty about the product—an approach generally read as consistent with the regulatory definition quoted in Mayrath footnote 4, although some practitioners argue that the "concept of a model" gloss at 590 should not be applied where it conflicts with the current regulatory definition. Specifically, physical build costs of a pilot model qualify only if the primary purpose of constructing the model was investigative—to test and resolve genuine design uncertainty—rather than merely constructing a functional building or fulfilling a commercial or personal occupancy requirement.
Defective Excess-Cost Valuation Approach and Substantiation Failures

A third critical failure in Mayrath was the taxpayer's top-down, macro-level accounting approach to quantifying his claimed R&E expenditures, paired with a complete lack of project-level nexus for his collateral deductions. Rather than tracking discrete experimental activities from the bottom up—by isolating specific engineering hours, laboratory tests, or destructive material trials linked to specific technical uncertainties—Mayrath employed a flawed "subtraction" or "excess-cost" formula. He aggregated the entire gross cost of constructing the Lennox Lane residence ($287,474.11), obtained a generalized estimate of what a conventional luxury home of similar square footage would cost ($116,520.00), and, treating the difference ($170,954.11 on the completed house) as attributable to experimentation, deducted the corresponding ratio of each year's construction outlays plus $4,000.00 of contractor accounting expense, for a total of $174,797.77 on the 1956 and 1957 returns, as deductible R&E under IRC § 174.

During the Tax Court trial, the overbreadth of this top-down allocation became evident through the petitioners' own concessions. Because Mayrath simply subtracted an arbitrary baseline from his total construction outlays, his claimed "research and experimental" deduction included cost ratios attributable to luxury carpeting, custom draperies, residential landscaping, a backyard swimming pool, and private tennis courts—items for which the petitioners conceded during trial additional amounts of $7,500.00 for 1956 and $35,000.00 for 1957 as nondeductible research and experimental expenditures. Furthermore, although Mayrath paid $4,000.00 in special accounting fees to his building contractor to segregate invoices labeled "special construction," the Tax Court noted that although this expense would seem to have enabled them to identify specific experimental costs, the petitioners instead presumed, without convincing proof, a $20-per-square-foot conventional cost—a method that lacked identification of specific expenditures and failed to assure that the costs of materials, labor, and other component elements of construction were excluded.

This evidentiary deficiency extended equally to Mayrath's collateral claims for 1955, 1956, and 1957. Regarding the claimed engineering and technical services ($3,350.00 in 1955), business services ($400.00 in 1955), and standalone R&E expenditures ($2,022.62 in 1956 and $1,904.43 in 1957), Mayrath offered only vague testimony, referring to checks and invoices that were never placed in evidence, and was unable to connect the alleged expenditures to a particular trade or business or specific project; he admitted some commingling with the house expenditures, most of the "research and experimental" materials were suitable for residential or other personal use, and the 1955 engineering and business-service amounts were payments to Truitt Bishop—from whom he bought the Cinderella Lane house and who drew the Lennox Lane plans—that he acknowledged partly covered the residence purchase, a large telephone bill, and architect fees. Similarly, with respect to his residential business-use allocations ($1,072.96 in 1955, $3,072.46 in 1956, and $3,365.40 in 1957), Mayrath claimed room-by-room percentage allocations across three personal residences in California, Cinderella Lane, and Lennox Lane based on storing music files for the dormant Christopher Music Co. and making occasional business telephone calls. Neither the Tax Court nor the Fifth Circuit accepted the passive storage of hobby records or sporadic residential phone calls as establishing bona fide business use over personal living quarters barred by IRC § 262. Finally, concerning the adjacent workshop depreciation ($700.00 in 1956 and $2,100.00 in 1957 on a structure he claimed had cost $42,000.00), Mayrath asserted that the workshop adjacent to his Lennox Lane residence was used for housing research, music printing experiments, and farm machinery work, yet the workshop's business use, actual cost, and useful life were all unsubstantiated by any documentary evidence; it was not established whether the alleged cost was already included in the residence cost, his only useful-life testimony was "We will probably tear it up in 20 years," and the Tax Court found it inconceivable that the one-story, 20-by-40-foot slab structure in a residential area had cost $42,000.00.
Threshold Failure of the Cohan Approximation Doctrine

Confronted with the collapse of his top-down subtraction formula and the absence of contemporaneous project records, Mayrath argued before the Fifth Circuit that both the Tax Court and the appellate court were legally obligated under Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930), to approximate and allow at least a minimum reasonable deduction for the experimental features of the house, the residential business uses, and the workshop depreciation. In Cohan, Judge Learned Hand established the rule that where a taxpayer proves he has incurred bona fide deductible business expenses, the complete disallowance of the deduction merely because the taxpayer cannot substantiate the exact dollar amount is impermissible; the trial court must make as close an approximation as it can, bearing heavily if it chooses upon the taxpayer whose inexactitude is of his own making.

The Fifth Circuit in Mayrath issued a definitive rebuke of this argument, articulating a strict two-step evidentiary gatekeeping standard that continues to govern R&D tax credit litigation today. Citing Williams v. United States, 245 F.2d 559 (5th Cir. 1957), Wiles v. United States, 312 F.2d 574 (10th Cir. 1962), and Oates v. Commissioner, 316 F.2d 56 (8th Cir. 1963), the Fifth Circuit held that the Cohan doctrine is wholly inapposite unless and until the taxpayer first satisfies the threshold burden of proving that at least some of the underlying expenditures were definitely deductible as bona fide business or research expenses.

As Senior Judge Jones explained, Cohan does not authorize or require a trial court to speculate as to whether an activity was connected with a trade or business and, applying the same reasoning to the § 174 house claim, that the taxpayer must first prove his expenses are truly deductible before any approximation of amount will be made. Because income tax deductions and credits are matters of legislative grace, statutory provisions authorizing them must be strictly and narrowly construed, and the burden rests squarely on the taxpayer to prove entitlement. Because Mayrath failed at the first step—proving that the Lennox Lane house or the adjacent workshop involved qualified, profit-motivated R&E or trade or business operations—he was legally barred from reaching the second step of using Cohan to estimate the quantum of deductible expenses. In modern IRC § 41 examinations and Tax Court trials (such as Eustace v. Commissioner, Betz v. Commissioner, and Little Sandy Coal), courts routinely apply this exact principle: if a taxpayer fails to prove at the business-component level that qualified research occurred under the four-part test (including the "substantially all" 80% threshold of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)), the court will refuse to invoke Cohan to salvage a partial credit.

Depreciable Property & Land Exclusion

Deducted a ratio-based share of the capital construction costs (materials, labor, and overhead) of a 5,826-sq-ft permanent building—initially including land improvements such as the swimming pool, tennis courts, and landscaping, whose costs were conceded at trial—directly as current § 174 expenses.

Standard: Capital expenditures to acquire or improve land or depreciable property are barred from § 174 expensing; even when research creates a depreciable end-product, component materials and construction labor are excluded. Holding: Disallowed in full; the Tax Court quoted § 174(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b) and faulted the method for failing to exclude materials and labor, but rested its holding on the absence of a trade or business, the non-research nature of the costs, and § 262, while the Fifth Circuit expressly declined to decide the § 174(c) question.

Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) and CCA 200013017, property of a character subject to depreciation cannot be claimed as a "supply" QRE unless it satisfies the strict "pilot model" rules of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) (T.D. 9680) where the sole purpose of build-out is resolving design uncertainty.
Prohibition on Personal, Living & Family Expenses

Constructed a 6-bedroom, 5-bathroom luxury home for immediate family occupancy; claimed percentage deductions across three residences (California, Cinderella Lane, Lennox Lane) for storing dormant music files and making phone calls.

Standard: IRC § 262 strictly bars personal, living, or family expenses; deductions are a matter of legislative grace and cannot be used to subsidize personal residences under the guise of R&D. Holding: Disallowed; allowing § 174 deductions for an occupied family residence would produce an absurd statutory result.

Dual-use assets (executive facilities, demonstration sites, founder workshops, or corporate aircraft/vessels) face heightened scrutiny; any personal or non-research utilization contaminates the business component unless strictly segregated.
Bottom-Up Cost Accounting & Nexus Substantiation
IRC § 174; IRC § 6001; Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2; Mayrath, 41 T.C. at 590–591.

Used a top-down "subtraction" method ($287,474.11 total cost minus $116,520.00 estimated conventional cost = $170,954.11 excess); deducted $4,000 of contractor accounting expense paid to record costs of "special construction" yet still relied on a presumed $20-per-square-foot baseline rather than identifying specific experimental costs.

Standard: Taxpayer must substantiate the direct nexus between specific expenditures and qualified investigative activities; macro-level excess-cost estimates that sweep in non-qualifying items (drapes, carpets, pools) are invalid. Holding: Subtraction formula and unsubstantiated engineering/workshop claims rejected in their entirety.

Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), taxpayers must substantiate QREs at the discrete "business component" level to prove the 80% "substantially all" threshold, or have granular data to apply the "shrink-back" rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2).
Threshold Prerequisite for Cohan Estimation
Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930); Williams v. United States, 245 F.2d 559 (5th Cir. 1957); Oates v. Commissioner, 316 F.2d 56 (8th Cir. 1963).

Demanded that the court apply Cohan to estimate and allow a minimum percentage of the $174,797.77 R&E claim, the workshop depreciation ($700 and $2,100 claimed on a structure allegedly costing $42,000), and residential expenses despite failing to prove any underlying business or research qualification.

Standard: Cohan estimation is legally inapplicable until the taxpayer first proves that the underlying activity is definitely deductible; courts will not speculate on unproven business or research connections. Holding: Application of Cohan rejected across all issues.

In modern R&D tax credit litigation (Betz, Eustace, Machise), post-hoc oral testimony and macro estimates cannot trigger Cohan unless contemporaneous technical documentation first proves that qualified experimentation occurred.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies
Case Study 1: Advanced Modular Structural Engineering and Custom Architectural Fabrication
Industry Scenario and Mayrath Vulnerability Profile

Apex Agri-Structures Corp. ("Apex"), a mid-market United States corporation headquartered in Texas with $65 million in annual gross receipts from manufacturing galvanized steel grain silos and agricultural material-handling conveyors, decides to expand into commercial net-zero, non-wood modular structural building systems. Apex constructs a two-story, 7,500-square-foot structural demonstration facility and executive conference center ("Project Horizon") on land adjacent to its corporate headquarters at a total cost of $4,200,000. The facility is built entirely without structural timber or traditional Portland cement, utilizing an experimental pultruded carbon-basalt composite framing system, phase-change thermal wall panels, and an automated subterranean greywater recycling matrix.

Upon completion, Apex's chief executive officer uses the second floor for executive board meetings, client entertainment, and overnight corporate guest lodging. To claim the IRC § 41 R&D tax credit and identify IRC § 174 specified research and experimental expenditures, Apex's controller estimates that a conventional steel-and-masonry commercial office building of 7,500 square feet would cost $1,800,000. Subtracting $1,800,000 from the $4,200,000 total outlay, Apex claims the entire $2,400,000 excess cost as qualified supply and contract research QREs under IRC § 41, relying on a single general ledger cost center labeled "Special Non-Wood Modular Construction".

Under an IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) examination, Project Horizon faces total disallowance under Mayrath v. Commissioner across three primary legal dimensions. First, regarding trade or business nexus and profit motive, Apex's established trade or business—like Martin Mayrath's—is agricultural handling equipment rather than commercial modular building construction; furthermore, using the completed structure for executive meetings and overnight guest lodging triggers IRC § 262 and § 274 personal and entertainment disallowances while negating pure laboratory intent. Second, under Mayrath (41 T.C. at 590), IRC § 174(c), Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(b)(2) and (4), and IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), the $2,400,000 excess cost represents the "actual construction" of a permanent, depreciable real property improvement (39-year nonresidential real property under IRC § 168), rather than "expenditures of an investigative nature expended in developing the concept of a model or product". Third, subtracting an estimated baseline building cost ($1,800,000) from total project outlays ($4,200,000) replicates Mayrath's invalidated top-down subtraction formula, sweeping in non-qualifying architectural finishes, HVAC installation, landscaping, and executive furnishings while failing the business-component and 80% "substantially all" tests of IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Protocol
Step 1: Corporate Governance and Commercial Trade or Business Nexus

To satisfy the judicial standards of Kenneth Reiner and Best Universal Lock Co. as articulated by the Fifth Circuit in Mayrath, Apex must establish an objective, pre-construction administrative record proving a bona fide commercial profit motive in the modular building systems sector prior to incurring any expenditures. Before breaking ground, Apex's Board of Directors must adopt a formal corporate resolution chartering the "Apex Modular Structural Technologies Division" with a dedicated commercial business plan, multi-year revenue projections, and a capital budget aimed specifically at licensing and manufacturing pultruded composite structural assemblies for third-party commercial developers. Concurrently, Apex must commission a documented commercial feasibility study identifying target commercial markets and retain external patent counsel at project inception to conduct prior-art searches and file provisional and non-provisional United States patent applications covering the carbon-basalt load-bearing joints and phase-change wall assemblies. Finally, Apex must eliminate all executive offices, conference rooms, and overnight guest quarters from the experimental structure; consistent with Kenneth Reiner, the structure must be operated exclusively as an uninhabited, instrumented structural testing laboratory and destructive/non-destructive test bed until all R&D phases are formally closed.
Step 2: Disaggregating Business Components and Applying the Shrink-Back Rule

To cure the fatal defect of Mayrath's "excess-cost subtraction" method and overcome the depreciable property bar of IRC § 174(c) and IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), Apex must abandon treating the entire building—or the "excess cost" of the building—as a single business component. Instead, under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and the shrink-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2), Apex must disaggregate the project into discrete, patentable sub-assemblies (the shrunk-back business components) where genuine technological uncertainty exists, completely excluding the surrounding building shell, foundation, land improvements, and interior build-out. Specifically, Apex should establish three separate business components: Business Component 1.1 (BC-1.1), the Pultruded Carbon-Basalt Snap-Lock Structural Beam-to-Column Node; Business Component 1.2 (BC-1.2), the Micro-Encapsulated Phase-Change Thermal Cladding Panel; and Business Component 1.3 (BC-1.3), the Closed-Loop Membrane Bioreactor Greywater Filtration Module.

By isolating these three discrete sub-assemblies as independent pilot models under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) (T.D. 9680), Apex ensures that no land, building foundation, conventional roofing, or depreciable real estate construction labor contaminates the QRE pool. To qualify the material costs of fabricating prototype iterations of BC-1.1, BC-1.2, and BC-1.3 as eligible pilot model supplies under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), Apex must build standalone, modular test rigs in its engineering laboratory first, subjecting them to destructive hydraulic load testing and thermal chamber cycling until destruction or scrap disposal—thereby satisfying CCA 200013017 so that the test units are never placed in service as depreciable property under IRC § 167 or § 168. If a full-scale structural assembly is subsequently erected outdoors to test multi-axis wind-shear and seismic resonance across interconnected nodes, only the discrete experimental nodes built solely to resolve structural design uncertainty—and permanently instrumented or dismantled post-testing—are tracked as pilot models, while all standard site preparation and facility construction costs are capitalized to non-R&D building accounts under IRC § 263(a).
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Process of Experimentation Tracking

To satisfy Mayrath's "investigative nature" standard (41 T.C. at 590) and the four-part test of IRC § 41(d)(1), Apex must implement a mandatory Stage-Gate Engineering Protocol that documents the scientific process of experimentation for each shrunk-back business component. At Gate 1 (Hypothesis and Technical Uncertainty Declaration), prior to Computer-Aided Design (CAD) modeling, the lead structural engineer must record a formal Technical Uncertainty Memorandum for BC-1.1 specifying why publicly available composite engineering standards cannot predict whether a wood-free, adhesive-free basalt-carbon joint can withstand 140-mph wind uplift and cyclic thermal expansion from -20°F to 130°F without delamination or shear fracture. At Gate 2 (Iterative Modeling and Simulation), the engineering team must maintain version-controlled CAD files and Finite Element Analysis (FEA) stress-simulation logs evaluating at least three distinct geometric joint configurations, such as dovetail locking versus tapered pin-shear versus pretensioned sleeve designs. At Gate 3 (Physical Prototype Trial and Failure Analysis), technicians must record empirical laboratory test data, strain-gauge telemetry, ultrasonic delamination scans, and formal failure analysis reports for each physical prototype iteration tested on the hydraulic load frame, documenting how specific test failures drove design modifications in subsequent iterations.
Step 4: Bottom-Up Cost Accounting and Contractual Structuring

Apex must replace its single "Special Construction" ledger account with a granular Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) in its Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system that enforces bottom-up cost capture. All internal structural engineers and metallurgy technicians must log daily hours contemporaneously into the ERP system against specific WBS phase codes that strictly distinguish Phase A (Conceptual Design, FEA Simulation, and Lab Testing, which constitute eligible IRC § 41 in-house wage QREs) from Phase B (Commercial Facility Erection, Site Supervision, and Quality Control, which constitute excluded construction labor under Mayrath and IRC § 41(d)(4)). Purchase orders for raw carbon fiber, basalt resin, and sacrificial test coupons consumed and destroyed during Phase A laboratory trials must be coded to a dedicated R&D Consumable Supplies sub-ledger, completely segregated from construction bills of materials.

Where Apex engages external structural testing laboratories or specialized composite fabricators to assist with BC-1.1 through BC-1.3, the written Master Services Agreements (MSAs) must be structured to avoid the "funded research" exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e). Specifically, the contracts must state that the services are performed on a time-and-materials or technical-milestone basis where Apex bears the full financial risk if the composite prototypes fail structural load tests, that Apex retains exclusive ownership and "substantial rights" to all resulting intellectual property, patents, and engineering data without paying any future royalty, and that the vendor's invoices itemize investigative engineering and destructive testing separately from any non-qualifying commercial fabrication.
Case Study 2: Semiconductor and Industrial Automation Custom Tooling and Pilot Line Development
Industry Scenario and Mayrath Vulnerability Profile

Precision Wafer Kinetics, LLC ("PWK"), a closely held domestic engineering and equipment manufacturing firm taxed as a corporation, generates $28 million annually manufacturing standard chemical vapor deposition (CVD) chambers for semiconductor foundries. PWK's majority shareholder and chief technologist constructs a $1,500,000, 4,000-square-foot detached high-bay workshop ("Annex B") adjacent to his private estate, approximately 15 miles from PWK's main manufacturing plant. Inside Annex B, the founder and four PWK engineers spend two tax years developing an experimental ultra-high-temperature silicon-carbide (SiC) epitaxial wafer annealing tool ("Project Hyperion"), while simultaneously using Annex B to restore the founder's vintage aviation engines and fabricate custom replacement parts for PWK's routine commercial warranty repairs.

Once the first full-scale Project Hyperion annealing chamber is assembled inside Annex B at a hardware and raw material cost of $950,000, PWK uses the chamber to process 500 commercial silicon-carbide wafers for a paying customer, generating $400,000 in commercial processing revenue, and subsequently retains the chamber as a permanent, revenue-generating foundry tool on its fixed-asset depreciation schedule. On its federal tax return, PWK claims $950,000 in supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) for the component materials used to build the Project Hyperion chamber, 100% of the wages ($820,000) of the founder and the four engineers based on an oral post-hoc estimate that "almost all of their time at Annex B was spent inventing," and § 174 R&E deductions for the utility, maintenance, and depreciation expenses of the $1,500,000 Annex B workshop. When the IRS demands timecards and project logs during examination, PWK invokes Cohan v. Commissioner, arguing that because Project Hyperion achieved a technological breakthrough, the IRS or Tax Court must estimate an allowable R&D credit.

Under Mayrath v. Commissioner and its modern IRC § 41 progeny (Union Carbide, Betz, Little Sandy Coal, and CCA 200013017), PWK's claim faces comprehensive disqualification. First, operating Annex B on the founder's residential estate while mixing vintage aviation engine restoration (a personal hobby under IRC § 262 and § 183), commercial warranty repairs (excluded post-production and quality control activities under IRC § 41(d)(4)), and R&D directly mirrors the disallowed depreciation on Mayrath's Lennox Lane workshop (allegedly built for $42,000). Second, under Mayrath (41 T.C. at 590), IRC § 174(c), IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), Union Carbide, and CCA 200013017, the $950,000 annealing chamber is tangible property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation under IRC §§ 167 and 168 that was placed into commercial service to process wafers sold in the ordinary course of business; consequently, its construction materials are capital expenditures rather than deductible R&E supplies. Third, under the Fifth Circuit's holding in Mayrath (357 F.2d at 214) and modern Tax Court precedent (Redelsheimer, Lockheed Martin, Max), PWK's failure to maintain contemporaneous records segregating qualified R&D from vintage aviation hobbies and commercial warranty work defeats the threshold requirement that expenses be proven definitely deductible—rendering Cohan completely inapplicable and disqualifying the executive and engineering wages under the 80% "substantially all" rule.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Protocol
Step 1: Facility Segregation and Elimination of Personal and Commercial Contamination

To eliminate the Mayrath workshop defect and IRC § 262 personal-expense contamination, PWK must physically and legally sever all R&D operations from the founder's residential estate and hobby activities. All Project Hyperion development must be moved out of the residential Annex B workshop and into a physically partitioned, access-controlled R&D Cleanroom and Prototyping Lab within PWK's commercial manufacturing facility, or into a dedicated commercial lease facility held strictly in PWK's corporate name. Furthermore, corporate governance policies must strictly prohibit any personal assets (such as vintage aviation components) or commercial warranty repair jobs from entering the R&D Prototyping Lab. If specialized metrology equipment (such as scanning electron microscopes) is shared between R&D and commercial quality control, depreciation allowances may only be claimed under IRC § 174 (and must be excluded from IRC § 41 per IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)) based on automated machine-hour badge logs, never as part of the IRC § 41 credit calculation.
Step 2: Navigating the Depreciable Property Rule for Prototype Tooling and Wafer Supplies

To salvage supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and overcome the depreciable property bar of Mayrath, IRC § 174(c), IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), and CCA 200013017, PWK must fundamentally restructure how it designs, tests, and disposes of prototype hardware and test wafers. Rather than building a single $950,000 commercial annealing chamber and placing it into depreciable foundry service, PWK must isolate the three high-risk technological subsystems where genuine thermal and fluid-dynamic uncertainty exists: the Inductive RF Graphite Susceptor Coil, the Laminar Argon Gas-Curtain Injector Manifold, and the Pyrometric Closed-Loop Thermal Controller. PWK should construct multiple iterative, bench-scale pilot models of these three sub-assemblies strictly to test whether they can maintain uniform wafer temperatures at 1,950°C ± 0.5°C without silicon sublimation or quartz chamber cracking.

Under CCA 200013017 and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), tangible prototype sub-assemblies and test wafers that are consumed, thermally warped, destructively sectioned for metallurgical microscopy, or scrapped following experimental trials are not property of a character subject to depreciation because they have no useful life in commercial production. PWK must institute a formal "R&D Scrap and Destructive Testing Certificate" signed by the quality assurance manager and tax director, documenting the physical destruction and disposal of each experimental coil, manifold, and test wafer batch. Once the experimental sub-assemblies resolve the thermal design uncertainties and PWK constructs the final full-scale chamber for commercial foundry operations, the capital cost of constructing that commercial chamber must be capitalized under IRC § 263(a) and depreciated under IRC § 168—explicitly excluded from both IRC § 41 supply QREs and IRC § 174 per Mayrath (41 T.C. at 590). Similarly, in strict compliance with Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner (697 F.3d 104) and CCA 200013017, any silicon-carbide wafers processed during experimental runs that are subsequently sold to customers must be excluded from supply QREs; only dedicated sacrificial test wafers that are destructively cleaved for epitaxial layer thickness measurement and discarded qualify as IRC § 41 supplies.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Time-Phased Substantiation to Overcome the Cohan Barrier

To prevent the disallowance of the $820,000 in engineering and executive wages under Mayrath's anti-Cohan rule and Redelsheimer, PWK must replace oral post-hoc estimates with contemporaneous, project-level time and activity tracking. All engineers—including the founder and chief technologist—must complete contemporaneous bi-weekly electronic timesheets allocating hours by specific Business Component (such as Susceptor Coil Pilot Model v1.0 and v2.0) and specific IRC § 41 activity category: Direct Qualified Research (thermal modeling, bench testing, failure analysis), Direct Supervision or Direct Support of Qualified Research under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c) (machining sacrificial test manifolds, calibrating pyrometers for specific experiments), and Non-Qualified Activities (commercial wafer processing, customer warranty servicing, general administrative management).

Because executive wage claims are routinely disallowed when unsupported by technical output (Redelsheimer), the founder must be documented as the author or reviewer on contemporaneous engineering change orders (ECOs), thermal simulation run logs, and laboratory test notebooks, establishing direct first-line supervision or hands-on experimentation rather than high-level financial oversight. By tracking time strictly against the shrunk-back sub-assembly pilot models (Susceptor Coil, Gas Injector, and Thermal Controller) and terminating the R&D project codes the moment the final design is released to commercial manufacturing under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), PWK ensures that well over 80% of the documented engineering hours per business component constitute a process of experimentation under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)—eliminating any need to rely on judicial approximation under Cohan.
Step 4: Contractual Risk Allocation for Customer Beta Testing

If PWK enters into an agreement with a semiconductor foundry customer to beta-test the Project Hyperion technology, PWK must structure the contract to avoid having the entire development deemed "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) or a routine commercial production contract under Little Sandy Coal. PWK must never bundle experimental equipment development with commercial wafer processing in a single cost-plus or fixed-price service contract. Instead, any commercial sale of an annealing system must be governed by a conditional prototype sales contract wherein payment is strictly contingent upon the tool achieving unprecedented, objectively verifiable technical performance specifications (such as achieving less than 1% epitaxial defect density at 1,950°C across a 200mm SiC wafer) following acceptance testing, and where PWK retains exclusive, unrestricted ownership and substantial rights to all underlying patents, firmware, and chamber designs.

cells: Business & Facility Nexus
Executing R&D inside personal residences or dual-use estate workshops without pre-existing commercial operations or market studies.
Formal corporate division charter, pre-project market feasibility studies, active patent prosecution, and dedicated, non-residential laboratory facilities.
IRC § 174(a); Mayrath, 357 F.2d at 212–214; Kenneth Reiner, 24 T.C.M. 1005; Best Universal Lock Co., 45 T.C. 1.
Asset & Prototype Qualification
Claiming capital construction costs of permanent buildings or revenue-generating production equipment as current R&D expenses or supplies.
Disaggregating projects via the shrink-back rule into discrete sub-assembly pilot models; executing documented destructive testing or scrap disposal.
Cost Quantification Approach
Top-down "subtraction" method (deducting total capital cost less estimated conventional baseline cost) or macro ratio allocations.
Bottom-up Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) tracking direct wages, sacrificial supplies, and qualifying contract costs by discrete business component.
Evidentiary Substantiation
Relying on oral post-hoc estimates, contractor "special construction" labels, and demanding judicial approximation under Cohan.
Contemporaneous bi-weekly project timesheets, Stage-Gate uncertainty memos, CAD/FEA logs, and empirical test failure reports proving qualification first.
IRC § 6001; Mayrath, 357 F.2d at 214; Williams v. United States, 245 F.2d 559; Max v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-37.

body.text: Conclusion and Strategic Advisory Synthesis

More than sixty years after its issuance, Mayrath v. Commissioner, 41 T.C. 582 (1964), aff'd, 357 F.2d 209 (5th Cir. 1966), remains a cornerstone of United States research and development tax law. While the superficial facts of the case involved an inventor's overreaching attempt to write off the construction of a custom, wood-free luxury family residence in Dallas, Texas, the legal principles forged by the Tax Court and the Fifth Circuit establish the exact doctrinal boundaries that govern multibillion-dollar corporate R&D tax credit disputes under IRC § 41 and capitalization audits under IRC § 174 today.

Three enduring mandates emerge from Mayrath for United States tax practitioners and corporate technical advisors. First, conceptual investigation must be strictly segregated from physical asset construction: under 41 T.C. at 590, the statutory boundary of IRC § 174—and thus the first prong of the IRC § 41 credit—is drawn firmly between expenditures of an investigative nature expended in developing the concept of a model or product and the actual construction of a functional asset. Whenever R&D intersects with custom manufacturing, architectural engineering, plant process improvements, or capital equipment builds, taxpayers cannot claim the physical build-out of a commercial or depreciable asset unless the specific component satisfies the strict "pilot model" criteria of Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4). Second, top-down "excess-cost" accounting is highly vulnerable: the Tax Court rejected Mayrath's subtraction of a presumed baseline cost from the total cost of his project because the method lacked identification of specific expenditures and failed to exclude materials, labor, and other construction costs, requiring taxpayers instead to construct bottom-up accounting trails tied to shrunk-back business components under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Third, the Cohan rule cannot rescue unproven qualification: judicial estimation under Cohan is never a substitute for proving the threshold statutory elements of a profit-motivated trade or business, technological uncertainty, and a scientific process of experimentation. Only through rigorous corporate governance, physical segregation of experimental facilities, bottom-up business-component cost accounting, and contemporaneous empirical test documentation can taxpayers satisfy the demanding burden of proof established in Mayrath v. Commissioner.

metaDescription: Mayrath v. Commissioner (1964): an inventor could not deduct the excess costs of building his experimental residence as IRC § 174 research expenses.
